criterion_notes.c1: Examines household domestic water service access (communal standpipes supplied by the Water Utilities Corporation, private connections, wells/boreholes, and rivers) in three rural villages in the Okavango Delta, Botswana.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines statutory water governance institutions (Water Act 1968, WUC Act 1970, Water Policy 2012, Land Boards) and customary institutions (taboos and traditional access rules). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly examines specific rule-type mechanisms governing household water access: (1) utility regulatory/ownership transfer from District Councils and the Department of Water Affairs (free rural standpipes) to the commercial parastatal Water Utilities Corporation (WUC) operating under statutory full cost-recovery rules, rising block tariffs, and connection fees; (2) statutory water-right permitting and annual abstraction fees (P3,400/year under the Water Act 1968) plus laborious Land Board land-right requirements to drill private wells/boreholes; and (3) customary rules and taboos restricting river/sacred source abstraction.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary mixed-methods empirical evidence from a household survey (n = 455 household heads), key informant interviews (44 village elders and 17 government officials), and focus group discussions conducted June–November 2018, analysed using descriptive statistics, Kruskal–Wallis and Mann–Whitney U tests, Pearson correlation, and thematic/content analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple household-level water access outcomes: water source used (85% standpipes, with 15% resorting to rivers due to tariffs), water affordability/expenditure share of monthly income (91.9% earning below BWP 1,500 spending up to 40% of income on water bills; significant differences across income groups), daily water consumption quantity (mean 75.4 L/day; 21.1% below recommended quantity), supply reliability/continuity, collection distance and time, and exclusion from private borehole ownership.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and household unit of analysis (455 households plus elders and officials in Shakawe, Tubu, and Shorobe), legal/institutional exposures (WUC cost-recovery tariffs/connection fees, Water Act permitting/fees, Land Board tenure rules, and customary taboos), household access outcomes, and cross-sectional mixed-methods study design.

evidence_quotes.quote: Adopting an expert and homogeneous purposive sampling procedure, a total of 455 household heads, 44 community elders and 17 government officials were sampled in three rural villages in the Okavango Delta.

Personal interview with a key informant in Shakawe revealed that the residents were now expected to pay for water obtained from communal standpipes (previously provided for free to all rural communities) just immediately after the DWA ceded responsibility of water supply to the WUC. This policy shift was justified on the ground that the WUC would need to recover service costs through the revenue generated from the sale of water.
Once a water right is acquired, an individual is expected to pay water taxes, which are water user fees based on how much abstraction is allowed.

However, most (91.9%) of them earned less than the minimum wage of BWP1500 per month and spent 40% of it on water bills. A relatively small percentage (8.1%) of the studied population, however, earned above BWP1500 per month and spent between 1.5 and 5% of their income on water bills.

As the lower income group spend on average more than 5% of their income on water, it is concluded that improved water supply is economically inaccessible to most of the people in the study area. Given that the more water an individual uses, the more they pay for the item, some (15%) of the households resorted to fetching water from the Okavango and Thamalakane rivers.

raw_response.exposure: Statutory water governance and rule-type access mechanisms—specifically the transfer of rural water supply to the commercial parastatal Water Utilities Corporation (WUC) with full cost-recovery block tariffs and connection fees (WUC Act 1970), water-right permits and P3,400 annual user fees (Water Act 1968), and Land Board land-right requirements to drill wells—alongside customary water access rules and taboos.
raw_response.outcome: Household water source used (communal standpipe vs. well/river switching), water affordability (percentage of household monthly income spent on water bills), daily household water consumption volume (litres), service continuity/reliability, collection distance and time, and exclusion from private borehole ownership.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural households in Shakawe, Tubu, and Shorobe villages in the Okavango Delta, Botswana (455 household heads surveyed, plus 44 village elders and 17 government officials in key informant interviews and focus group discussions; primary unit of analysis: household).
raw_response.rationale: This primary mixed-methods empirical study in three rural villages in Botswana's Okavango Delta meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. It empirically examines how statutory rule-type mechanisms—transfer of rural standpipe provision to the commercial parastatal WUC under full cost-recovery block tariffs and connection fees, Water Act permitting and annual abstraction fees (P3,400/year), and Land Board land-tenure requirements for drilling wells—alongside customary taboos affect household water affordability, daily consumption quantity, reliability, collection burden, and reliance on unimproved river water.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods study (household survey, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions)
